description: Marxist, interactionist and feminist theories of crime: Chambliss, Becker, Heidensohn and Carlen.
content_html:
Beyond Functionalism: Conflict and Interactionist Theories

The previous lesson examined functionalist and subcultural explanations of crime. This lesson turns to three perspectives that challenge the functionalist premise that law and enforcement serve shared social interests: Marxism, interactionism and feminism. Each argues that who gets labelled “criminal” depends not simply on what a person does, but on their class, gender and ethnic position in a patriarchal and class-divided society.

Chambliss: Differential Enforcement of the Law

William Chambliss, in his landmark study Saints and Roughnecks (1973), provided one of the most vivid demonstrations of how social class shapes the application of the law. Chambliss observed two groups of adolescent boys in a small American town over two years. The “Saints” were eight middle-class boys who regularly truanted, drank and engaged in petty crime. The “Roughnecks” were six working-class boys with similar or lower levels of actual rule-breaking. Despite this, the Roughnecks were consistently stopped, arrested and prosecuted by police; the Saints were almost never. Teachers, police and community members viewed the Saints as “good boys having fun” and the Roughnecks as “headed for trouble.”

Chambliss argued that this pattern illustrates differential enforcement of the law: the law is applied selectively according to the class and social characteristics of the person, not just the act they commit. The Saints’ respectable appearance, access to cars (giving them mobility) and middle-class presentation made them less visible to the police and less likely to be labelled. The Roughnecks’ working-class presentation and visible presence in the town centre made them easy targets for police scrutiny.

Chambliss’s study bridges Marxist and interactionist perspectives. From a Marxist standpoint, the differential enforcement reflects the class bias built into the structure of the criminal justice system: the bourgeoisie shapes law enforcement to protect its interests. From an interactionist standpoint, the study shows how stereotypes shape the labelling process at the micro level of police-citizen encounters.

Key Fact

Chambliss (Saints and Roughnecks, 1973) compared two groups of adolescent boys with similar actual offending behaviour. The working-class Roughnecks were repeatedly arrested while the middle-class Saints were largely left alone. The study demonstrates differential enforcement of the law: the law is applied selectively according to class position, not just criminal behaviour.

The Interactionist Challenge: Becker’s Labelling Theory

Howard Becker, in Outsiders (1963), set out the foundational argument of labelling theory. Becker argued that deviance is not a property of the act itself but of the interaction between the person who acts and those who observe and respond to the act. Whether a label of “deviant” or “criminal” is applied depends on who commits the act, when and where it is committed, who observes it, and the negotiations between the various parties involved.

Once a label has been publicly and officially applied, Becker argued, it tends to become the person’s master status. Before the label, a young person might be seen as a student, a friend, a neighbour. After being officially convicted and labelled a “criminal”, this identity overshadows all others and can follow them into every interaction — with employers, landlords, teachers and family members.

The consequences of master status may trigger what Becker called a deviant career. As the labelled individual is rejected from legitimate social roles, the label itself makes conventional life harder to sustain. This can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy: the individual increasingly identifies with the label and seeks out others who share it.

Primary deviance refers to the original act of rule-breaking before any label has been applied. Secondary deviance occurs when an individual internalises the deviant label and begins to act in accordance with it. The distinction is important: secondary deviance is produced not by the original act but by the social reaction to it.

Becker introduced the concept of moral entrepreneurs — individuals and groups who use their social influence to get particular behaviours defined as deviant. Related to this is the concept of a moral panic: when the media, police and public respond to a perceived threat in a disproportionate and amplified way, the resulting attention can itself increase the visible scale of the problem through deviancy amplification. Critics argue that moral panics have historically targeted specific groups (young working-class men, ethnic minority communities) who are portrayed as “folk devils” — symbols of social threat.

Feminist Theories: Heidensohn and Carlen

Frances Heidensohn, in Women and Crime (1985), offered a feminist explanation for one of the most consistent patterns in crime data: women commit far fewer crimes than men. Rather than explaining this through biology or individual character, Heidensohn argued that women are subject to far more intensive social control than men, making it structurally more difficult for them to deviate. She identified three domains of patriarchal control:

  • In the home: Women are expected to spend the majority of their time on domestic labour and childcare. Those who challenge these expectations risk male violence as an assertion of patriarchal authority. Daughters are controlled more strictly than sons — earlier curfews, more restrictions on movement.
  • In public: Women face the threat of male sexual violence in public spaces, acting as an informal deterrent against independent movement. The cultural idea of “separate spheres” means that women who occupy public space in non-conforming ways may face ridicule or harassment.
  • At work: Women are controlled by male-dominated hierarchies and subjected to various forms of sexual harassment, limiting their organisational autonomy.

Heidensohn’s argument is that women’s lower crime rates are not evidence of superior morality but the result of more intensive control that restricts their opportunities to offend. Sociologists also note the chivalry thesis — the argument that women who conform to feminine stereotypes are treated more leniently by the criminal justice system than men committing similar offences. However, feminist criminologists argue that women who deviate from expected gender roles may conversely be judged more harshly.

Pat Carlen, in Women, Crime and Poverty (1988), studied 39 working-class women who had been convicted of criminal offences. Carlen draws on control theory but foregrounds class alongside gender. She argues that women are controlled through two kinds of deal. The class deal promises working-class women consumer goods and a respectable lifestyle in exchange for their labour. The gender deal offers psychological and material rewards through a male breadwinner in exchange for love and domestic labour. When either or both deals break down — through unemployment, poverty or abusive relationships — crime becomes a rational choice because the usual incentives for conformity are absent.

Key Fact

Heidensohn (Women and Crime, 1985) argues women commit fewer crimes because patriarchal control in the home, public and workplace restricts their opportunities to offend. Carlen (Women, Crime and Poverty, 1988) argues women turn to crime when the class deal and the gender deal both break down, removing the usual incentives for conformity.

Marxist / Chambliss: Strength is the clear empirical evidence of differential enforcement; limitation is that not all class-based policing differences are so stark, and Chambliss’s small US study may not generalise broadly. Interactionist / Becker: Shows how labelling processes operate at the micro level; criticised for not explaining why labels fall on the working class without reference to class power (Marxist critique). Not everyone who is labelled becomes a career criminal (over-deterministic). Feminist / Heidensohn and Carlen: Important corrective to male-centred criminology; Heidensohn has been criticised for making generalisations that do not apply equally to all women across class, ethnicity and age. Carlen’s small sample size limits generalisation. Both perspectives highlight that the sociology of crime cannot ignore gender.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about labelling theory, students often describe what a label is but neglect what it does: the consequences of master status, the self-fulfilling prophecy and the deviant career. A strong answer needs both the process (who applies labels, under what conditions) and the consequences. For the 12-mark Evaluate, the highest-scoring answers contrast at least two perspectives — for example, Becker’s interactionist focus on the reaction of others with Chambliss’s Marxist argument that class power determines whose reactions carry weight. Heidensohn is a named sociologist that many students describe too vaguely: be specific about her three domains of control (home, public, work) and link the argument to the broader feminist critique of patriarchal social structure. A supported judgement weighing the evidence is required for the Mastering tier.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Chambliss (Saints and Roughnecks, 1973) demonstrated differential enforcement of the law: working-class boys were consistently arrested for similar or lesser offending than middle-class boys, showing that class position shapes how the law is applied.
  • Becker’s labelling theory (Outsiders, 1963) argues that deviance is not a quality of the act but is created by social reactions. A master status, deviant career and self-fulfilling prophecy can result from the labelling process. Primary deviance is the original act; secondary deviance follows from internalising the label.
  • Heidensohn (Women and Crime, 1985) explains female conformity through patriarchal control in the home, public spaces and work. Carlen (Women, Crime and Poverty, 1988) argues women turn to crime when the class deal and gender deal both break down. Both feminist accounts challenge male-centred criminology.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best summarises the finding of Chambliss's Saints and Roughnecks study?
A) Working-class boys committed more crime than middle-class boys in the study
B) Middle-class boys were arrested more often because they were more visible to the police
C) Despite similar levels of offending, working-class boys were consistently arrested while middle-class boys were not
D) The study found no significant difference in how police treated the two groups
practice_questions.marks: C) Despite similar levels of offending, working-class boys were consistently arrested while middle-class boys were not [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'differential enforcement of the law'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that the law is applied unequally across social groups. 1 mark for specifying the basis of the inequality: working-class individuals are more likely to be stopped, arrested and prosecuted than middle- or upper-class individuals committing similar acts; the enforcement reflects social characteristics rather than solely the nature of the offence. Example: 'Differential enforcement of the law refers to the unequal application of criminal law, in which working-class individuals are more likely to be targeted by police and prosecution than middle-class individuals committing equivalent acts.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe how a deviant career may develop following the application of a criminal label.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the deviant career as the process by which a labelled individual is progressively drawn into a deviant identity. 2 marks for a developed description: the labelled person is excluded from legitimate opportunities (employment, housing, education) because the master status precedes them; this makes conventional life harder, producing a self-fulfilling prophecy; the individual increasingly identifies with the label and joins organised deviant groups, completing what Becker called the deviant career.

practice_questions.text: Describe Heidensohn's feminist explanation for women's lower rates of criminal behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying Heidensohn's argument that women face more intensive patriarchal control than men, making it harder to deviate. 1 mark for describing control in the home: domestic expectations, male violence as an assertion of authority, financial dependence on male breadwinners. 1 mark for control in public: threat of male sexual violence, separate spheres ideology limiting independent movement. 1 mark for control at work: male-dominated hierarchies, sexual harassment and limited organisational power. Or: 2 marks for two well-developed domains of control with clear explanation of how each restricts women's opportunities to offend.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that it is the reaction of others, not the act itself, that makes someone a criminal.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: interactionist evidence (Becker, Outsiders 1963) that the same act receives different labels depending on who commits it and who observes; Chambliss (Saints and Roughnecks 1973) showing class-based differential enforcement; crime statistics reflect policing practices as much as actual offending. Against or qualifying: Merton's strain theory argues that structural conditions, not reactions alone, cause crime; functionalists argue some acts are universally condemned regardless of who commits them; Marxist critique that labelling theory describes but does not explain why labels fall on the working class without reference to class power. Student names at least Becker plus one contrasting perspective and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered with named theorists, judgement present. Developing: mostly one perspective with limited evaluation. Emerging: basic descriptions, few theorists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations for why women commit fewer crimes than men.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. Relevant explanations: Heidensohn (Women and Crime, 1985) — patriarchal control in home, public and work restricts women's opportunities; Carlen (Women, Crime and Poverty, 1988) — class and gender deals break down for some women, making crime a rational choice; functionalist gender socialisation — boys socialised to be aggressive and risk-taking, girls to be conformist; chivalry thesis — criminal justice system treats women more leniently when they conform to feminine stereotypes. Critiques: Heidensohn's account does not explain all women equally (varies by class, ethnicity, age); Carlen's small sample limits generalisation; female offending rates have changed since 1985; the chivalry thesis is contested (women who deviate from gender norms may face harsher treatment). Student names at least Heidensohn and Carlen, presents multiple perspectives, weighs the evidence and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What did Chambliss's Saints and Roughnecks study (1973) demonstrate?
options: Working-class boys commit more crime than middle-class boys
Middle-class boys are more likely to be labelled as delinquent by their peers
The law is applied differentially according to class position, not just actual offending
Police arrests are determined solely by the seriousness of the offence

knowledge_checks.q: According to Becker, what is the primary factor that determines whether an act becomes labelled as deviant?
options: The seriousness of harm caused by the act
The social class of the person who commits the act
Whether the act breaks a formal law
The reaction and labelling process of others with the power to make the label stick

knowledge_checks.q: In labelling theory, _____ deviance is the original rule-breaking act before any label has been publicly applied.
Carlen argued that women turn to crime when both the _____ deal and the gender deal break down.
Match each sociologist to their key argument about crime:
right: Differential enforcement: working-class boys arrested for similar offences that middle-class boys escape
Deviance is not a quality of the act but is created by the reactions and labels applied by others
Women commit fewer crimes because patriarchal control restricts their opportunities to offend

flashcard_questions.q: Who conducted the Saints and Roughnecks study and in what year?
What did the Saints and Roughnecks study show about differential enforcement?
flashcard_questions.a: Working-class Roughnecks were repeatedly arrested; middle-class Saints were largely ignored despite similar offending levels.

flashcard_questions.q: What is differential enforcement of the law?
flashcard_questions.a: The unequal application of criminal law, with working-class individuals more likely to be stopped, arrested and prosecuted than others committing similar acts.

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote 'Outsiders' and in what year?
What is a master status, according to Becker?
flashcard_questions.a: A label that overrides all other social identities, becoming the primary way others see and respond to a person.
The process by which a labelled person is excluded from conventional roles, internalises the label and is drawn deeper into deviance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary deviance?
flashcard_questions.a: Primary deviance is the original act before labelling; secondary deviance follows from internalising the label and acting accordingly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Heidensohn's core argument about female conformity?
flashcard_questions.a: Women commit fewer crimes because patriarchal control in the home, public spaces and workplace restricts their opportunities to offend.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two deals Carlen identified that control women?
flashcard_questions.a: The class deal (consumer goods via wage) and the gender deal (rewards via male partner).

flashcard_questions.q: What does Carlen argue happens when both deals break down?
flashcard_questions.a: Crime becomes a rational choice because the usual incentives for conformity are absent.
The argument that women who conform to feminine stereotypes are treated more leniently by the criminal justice system than men.
A period of disproportionate public anxiety in which a group is defined as a threat to social values, typically amplified by media coverage.

glossary_terms.definition: The unequal application of criminal law, in which working-class individuals are more likely to be stopped, arrested and prosecuted than middle- and upper-class individuals committing similar acts.
A label that overrides all other social identities, becoming the primary way in which others see and respond to a person.
The process by which a labelled person is progressively excluded from conventional roles and drawn further into a deviant identity and lifestyle.
An initial rule-breaking act before any public label has been applied, so it does not alter the individual's social identity.
Deviance that results from internalising a publicly applied label and beginning to act in accordance with the deviant identity it imposes.
In Carlen's theory, the implicit bargain in which working-class women accept their position in exchange for consumer goods through their own wage.
In Carlen's theory, the implicit bargain in which women accept domestic labour and dependence in exchange for rewards provided by male partners.
A period of disproportionate public anxiety in which a group is portrayed as a threat to social values, typically amplified by media coverage.
The argument that women who conform to feminine stereotypes tend to be treated more leniently by the criminal justice system than men committing similar offences.

hero_image_caption: A courtroom interior — the site where labels are formally applied and where class, gender and ethnicity shape outcomes in ways Chambliss, Becker and Heidensohn each examined.
